summary.text: The Wiener process, also called Brownian motion, is a real-valued continuous-time stochastic process named after Norbert Wiener.
A time step u gives an increment that is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance u, its paths are almost surely continuous, and increments over separate periods are independent.
It appears in pure and applied mathematics, economics, quantitative finance, evolutionary biology and physics, and it gave rise to the study of continuous time martingales.

facts.label: Step size rule
facts.value: A time step u gives an increment with mean 0, variance u

facts.label: Built from
facts.value: Scaling limit of a random walk (Donsker's theorem)

facts.label: Path shape
facts.value: Unbounded variation, so not absolutely continuous

facts.label: Coming back
facts.value: Recurrent in one or two dimensions, not in three or more

items.prompt: A Wiener process is watched for a short step, and then for a step four times as long. How does the variance of its change compare?

options.label: The longer step has the same variance
The longer step has twice the variance
The longer step has four times the variance
The longer step has sixteen times the variance

items.explain: A time step u gives an increment with variance u, so the variance grows in proportion to the length of the step.

items.prompt: You watch a Wiener process climb sharply during the first hour. What does that say about its change in a separate, later hour?

options.label: It tells you nothing, because changes over separate periods are independent
It must fall back, to make up for the climb
It must keep climbing at the same pace
It must stay still, as the process has used up its motion

items.explain: The process has independent increments: changes over non-overlapping time periods are independent random variables.

items.prompt: A walker flips a coin for each step. If the steps are made smaller and faster in the right way, what does the walk approach?

options.label: A straight line
A fixed point it never leaves
A process that always moves one way
The Wiener process

items.explain: The Wiener process can be built as the scaling limit of a random walk, a result known as Donsker's theorem.

items.prompt: Two random wanderers follow Wiener processes, one moving on a flat floor and one flying through a room. Which one keeps returning near its start?

options.label: The wanderer on the floor
The flying wanderer
Both of them equally
Neither of them ever does

items.explain: The Wiener process is recurrent in one or two dimensions, but not in three or higher.

items.prompt: An electronics engineer wants to model random noise as the running total of white Gaussian noise. Which process fits?

options.label: A straight-line trend
A Wiener process
A coin that always lands heads
A fixed repeating wave

items.explain: The Wiener process is used to represent the integral of a white noise Gaussian process, so it is useful as a model of noise in electronics engineering.

items.prompt: Could the path of a Wiener process be recorded as an ordinary running total of some fixed function ξ?

options.label: Yes, any continuous path can be written that way
Yes, but only over very short time spans
No, its paths have unbounded variation
No, because its paths are never continuous

items.explain: Its paths have unbounded variation and are not absolutely continuous, so Wₜ cannot be represented as an integral over a function ξ.
